Sharing an NBA court should give them plenty more opportunities to build on that. The pair will put that chemistry to the test when the Sixers open the regular season against the defending champion Knicks on Oct. 20 at Madison Square Garden.

stories.title: What is Sam Hauser’s role?
stories.summary: The Celtics have added a bunch of wings over the past few years and they all can play, so where does that leave Hauser?
stories.detailText: BOSTON, MA - APRIL 28: Sam Hauser #30 of the Boston Celtics is introduced before the game against the Philadelphia 76ers on April 28, 2026 at TD Garden in Boston, Massachusetts. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Babineau/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images The 2023, 2024 and 2025 drafts all saw the Celtics select wings with their top pick. In all three cases, they found contributing players in Jordan Walsh, Baylor Scheierman and Hugo Gonzalez. With Jayson Tatum and Paul George being the starters on the wing, it leaves a murky role for Sam Hauser. Hauser even said that the young wings are looking good. “Jordan, Baylor, Hugo, Ron [Harper Jr.] all throughout this point in training camp have looked really good,” Hauser said at his media availability on Tuesday. “That’s awesome for our team because those four guys bring a different dynamic to what we’re trying to do. We’re excited to see what they can do for us throughout the year.” Sam Hauser still matters — he is Boston’s best catch and shoot guy and Jayson Tatum has always elevated his game. According to StatMuse, in games that Jayson Tatum did not play, Hauser shot 40.3% from three. In games that Tatum did play, Hauser shot 41.7% from three. According to databallr, since the start of the 2022-23 season, the Celtics offensive rating with just Tatum and no Hauser on the court is 121.2; when Hauser and Tatum share the court, that number jumps to 123.7. The Celtics are going to run their ‘Jayson Tatum plus the bench’ lineups this year. Those lineups should include Hauser, whose spacing helps those lineups a lot. In the Celtics first preseason game, Hauser came off of the bench. He played 21 minutes and had 11 points on 4/6 from the field and 3/5 from three. Boston used him in different ways than they typically do as well. pic.twitter.com/65MD9eYSab — #LetsGoCeltics (@gobosceltics) October 12, 2026 — #LetsGoCeltics (@gobosceltics) October 12, 2026 Last year was Hauser’s worst 3-point percentage of his career at 39%, still a very good number but not in the 40’s which we have become accustomed to. His shooting is so valuable to this Celtics team. While Walsh, Scheierman and Gonzalez are all good players that could push Hauser out of town eventually, the reason he remains a Celtic is his three-point shot. His ability to shoot standing still and off of movement is so important to what Boston does. Defenses have to respect him as a shooter because he will burn them if they don’t. For a team that takes as many threes as Boston does, Hauser plays a key role. However, it does need to be mentioned that Boston’s three young wings do a lot of things that Hauser does not do. They are all better defenders than Hauser is, they all offensive rebound better than Hauser does and both Scheierman and Gonzalez have shown that they can play with the ball in their hands more than Hauser can. That’s not to say that Hauser is a bad defender — they don’t call it ‘Hauser Island’ for no reason. Or that he can’t dribble at all; it’s just that the younger wings on the roster have proven to be better at it than Sam is. As Hauser also said at his media availability, everyone is going to have a chance to prove they belong on the court. “Pretty much throughout Joe’s coaching career to this point, I feel like one through seventeen we’ve all had a chance to play, all have had a chance to play good minutes and contributed to a lot of wins throughout the years,” he said. “The next man up mentality has kind of been our thing.” Hauser is on a very tradable contract. He is owed $35 million over the next 3 years and $10.8 million this year. Boston is currently $10.3 million under the first apron, where they are hard-capped due to the Mitchell Robinson signing. The C’s have a $27.7 million trade exception from the Anfernee Simons trade last February they can use to acquire someone. If they pair Hauser’s money with the exception and some of the draft capital they got for Jaylen Brown, the Celtics can make a difference making trade at the deadline if they so choose. The Celtics are going to need Sam Hauser this year. His catch and shoot game is too valuable for him not to be a fact on this team. However, with some younger wings on the roster, Hauser’s time in Boston could be coming to an end sooner rather than later. Even if most of Hauser’s time as a Celtic is done, he will still help the Celtics win basketball games as long as he is in green.

stories.title: Sources: 76ers' G League affiliate in Delaware tabs Brad Jones as GM
stories.summary: The Delaware Blue Coats, the 76ers' G League affiliate, are hiring Brad Jones as their next general manager, team sources told ESPN.
stories.detailText: The Delaware Blue Coats, the Philadelphia 76ers ' G League affiliate, are hiring Brad Jones as their next general manager, team sources told ESPN. Jones was selected, sources said, by Sixers president Mike Gansey and executive vice president of basketball operations Jameer Nelson, after former Blue Coats GM Ariana Andonian left to run the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks last month. Jones began his career with the Orlando Magic when Nelson played there, working his way up from being an intern to serving on the video and personnel staff. He most recently has worked in the G League offices in New York for the past eight years and was involved in player contracts and transactions, basketball operations and basketball affairs and player personnel. Delaware went 18-18 last season. The Blue Coats will open the 2026-27 G League season on Nov. 6 at home against the Capital City Go-Go.

stories.title: Kentavious Caldwell-Pope could be the Sixers’ secret weapon this season
stories.summary: KCP could wind up making a quietly big impact on the Sixers both on and off the court.
stories.detailText: CAMDEN, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 28: Kentavious Caldwell-Pope #1 of the Philadelphia 76ers poses for a portrait during media day at the Philadelphia 76ers Training Complex on September 28, 2026 in Camden, New Jersey. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images LeBron James and Jaylen Brown aren’t the only former NBA champions whom the Sixers added to their roster this offseason. Shortly after landing LeBron, they also signed Kentavious Caldwell-Pope to a one-year, veteran-minimum contract. KCP has largely gotten lost in the shuffle of the Sixers’ offseason overhaul, particularly coming off back-to-back disappointing seasons. But he might wind up being their secret weapon both on and off the court. Caldwell-Pope won a championship alongside LeBron with the 2019-20 Los Angeles Lakers, and he added a second ring a few years later with Nikola Jokić and the Denver Nuggets. He was a role player on both of those teams, which should give him a unique perspective to add in the Sixers’ locker room this year. Not only has KCP played with two of the greatest players of this generation, but he’s gotten to see the secret sauce behind two recent title teams. At the Sixers’ media day , Caldwell-Pope spoke about how important it is for the team to build off-court camaraderie, and how that helped fuel both the 19-20 Lakers and 22-23 Nuggets. LeBron’s back-and-forth trips to New York City might not be helping much in that regard right now, but once the season starts and the Sixers start heading out on extended road trips, they’ll have plenty of chances to bond throughout the 82-game grind. KCP isn’t just the Sixers’ honorary Kyle Lowry this season, though. There’s a chance that he’ll be able to make an impact on the court, too. From 2019-20 through 2023-24, Caldwell-Pope averaged 10.7 points per game while shooting 45.0 percent overall and 40.3 percent from deep. Over the past two seasons, he averaged only 8.6 points per game while shooting 42.7 percent overall and 33.3 percent from distance. At media day, KCP declared that his shot is still “great” and that he did a ton of shooting this past summer to get ready for this season. He also explained why he didn’t experience the success in Orlando and Memphis over the last two years that he did in L.A. and Denver. “For me, I’m a rhythm player,” he said. “I have to be in a rhythm, being able to touch the ball, being able to feel the ball. Last few teams, that wasn’t happening how I wanted it to happen. But I still got there and played my ass off defensively, gave it my all on both ends. “But I think here, just playing with these types of guys—Bron, JB, Joel, Maxey—it’s gonna be a lot of open shots, a lot of opportunity to be able to get back to shooting 40 percent. That plays a big part in me shooting 40 percent. I’ve gotta be able to get the ball, be in a rhythm. I think this team is gonna create those opportunities for us.” Caldwell-Pope underwent surgery in February to “ address a misalignment ” of his right pinkie finger. He said that was “probably the longest I had ever sat out” throughout his 13-plus-year NBA career, but he added that “my game is still there.” Since KCP is on a one-year, veteran-minimum deal, this was basically a risk-free signing for the Sixers. Anfernee Simons figures to be their sixth man, while Caldwell-Pope and rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. will battle for any leftover minutes behind Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe. If all of them play well, perhaps they’ll be able to convince head coach Nick Nurse to experiment with some three-guard lineups. That isn’t the only way KCP could help the Sixers on the court, though. If he puts his recent struggles behind him, he could open the door to a larger midseason shakeup, too. Simons signed a two-year, $12.3 million contract with the Sixers this summer, which includes a second-year player option. If he stays healthy and plays well, the Sixers might not be able to re-sign him next summer. Since the Sixers are in a win-now window, they aren’t likely to preemptively dump Simons for draft capital at the trade deadline to avoid losing him for nothing in free agency. But if KCP plays well enough to give them confidence in a Maxey-Edgecombe-KCP-Philon backcourt rotation, the Sixers could use Simons’ $6.0 million salary as a way to solve one of their other roster problems. (Such as, say, backup center ?) Of course, last year’s trade deadline is a great example of how quickly such a trade can backfire. Shortly after the Sixers traded Jared McCain for the first-round pick that they’d later use on Philon along with three second-rounders, Maxey suffered a finger injury that sidelined him for two weeks in March. The Sixers were down to Edgecombe, Quentin Grimes, Cameron Payne and Lowry as their only healthy backcourt options. This year’s Sixers do have Caleb Love and Rayan Rupert on two-way deals as well, and they shouldn’t have to be quite as reliant on their two-way players this season as they were last year. (In other words, they shouldn’t hit their 50-game limit as early.) Either way, their backcourt depth does look like a clear strength for them heading into the season. If Caldwell-Pope does have a bounce-back year, that could have some quietly huge implications for the Sixers heading into the February trade deadline and the spring. Unless otherwise noted, all stats via NBA.com , PBPStats , Cleaning the Glass or Basketball Reference . All salary information via Spotrac and salary-cap information via RealGM . Follow Bryan on Bluesky .

teamStories.title: 2026 NBA free agency: Grades for offseason signings, extensions
teamStories.summary: We're grading the biggest offseason signings, including Payton Pritchard's two-year extension with the Celtics.
teamStories.detailText: The NBA offseason still features plenty of important moves across the league. I'm grading every free agent signing and the most impactful extensions, breaking down the ramifications for all teams and players involved. To determine each grade, I'm looking at multiple factors, including the player's on-court impact and age, the contract's financial implications and the context of the team's short- and long-term outlooks. How risky or certain is the move? And how much does it help or hurt the team's chance to win a championship, next season or beyond? Let's get into the latest moves: Quick links: Trade grades | Latest buzz | Trade machine Depth charts | Trade tracker | More coverage Oct. 13: Pritchard lands two-year extension Payton Pritchard terms: Two years, $44.2 million Grade: A This deal is an easy grade for Boston, as Pritchard's production makes him worth considerably more. The 2024-25 Sixth Man of the Year averaged a career-high 17.0 points and 5.2 assists per game last season, is a career 39% 3-point shooter and has scored with above-average efficiency in five of his six NBA campaigns. Yet because Pritchard is currently playing on such a team-friendly contract -- $30 million over four years -- he was limited to a $22.1 million annual salary for his next extension. There was also the possibility that Pritchard could decline to sign a new below-market contract and test free agency in 2028, but he will now be guaranteed more than double his career earnings without the risk of anything going awry over the next two years. This extension carries little downside for Boston. Perhaps Pritchard will start to decline on his new deal, as he'll be a 30-year-old small guard by the time it begins, but he's far more likely to outplay it with the value he provides the Celtics. Marks: NBA extension decisions to watch this week Oct. 10: Warriors sign Podziemski to five-year extension Brandin Podziemski terms: Five years, $110 million Grade: B- As I wrote recently when explaining why Podziemski is a candidate to make ESPN's NBA Rank top 100 next season, the Warriors guard is underrated because he's a jack of all trades, master of none . Podziemski is a good shooter, a good passer and a good defender, but he's not amazing at any of those skills, which means he profiles more as a quality role player than a long-term star. An average annual salary of $22 million is a reasonable deal for that level of player, especially one in his early 20s. And the advanced metrics like Podziemski even more than his surface stats or reputation suggest. This deal also fits into the Warriors' plans for next summer. According to ESPN's Anthony Slater, Podziemski's new deal will start at $18.9 million in the first year before increasing in subsequent seasons. Given that Podziemski would have had a cap hold of $17 million if he hadn't signed an extension, this extension will shave less than $2 million off the Warriors' cap space next offseason. However, a five-year commitment at this figure is a lot for a role player. That length for a rookie extension is more typically reserved for players with more star-level upside -- such as Amen and Ausar Thompson , and Keyonte George this summer -- so the Warriors' grade for this deal slips down a notch, compared to if it had been a four-year agreement instead. Oct. 1: Duren signs five-year deal with Pistons Jalen Duren terms: Five years, $200 million Grade: B Your opinion of Duren's new contract rests on one key question: How severely do you penalize him for one bad postseason? At the end of the regular season, Duren seemed like a shoo-in to receive at least a $200 million deal. He was a deserving All-Star and All-NBA third-team honoree, averaging 19.5 points and 10.5 rebounds. He helped lead the Pistons to 60 wins and the No. 1 seed in the Eastern Conference. His 69% true shooting mark was by far the best in NBA history for a player with an above-average usage rate. And Duren even played well without Cade Cunningham , showing that the center's production was not solely a product of his point guard's brilliance. The Pistons had a plus-11.5 net rating when Duren played without Cunningham, per databallr, as well as a plus-11.5 net rating when the two played together. Detroit's net rating fell to plus-7.6 when Cunningham played without Duren. But then came the playoffs, and Duren looked like a completely different player: less confident, less assertive, less impactful. This wasn't a matter of one bad game or one tricky matchup; rather, he struggled across 14 games, against two very different opponents. Compared to the regular season, Duren averaged 9.3 fewer points in the playoffs. That's the largest drop for an All-Star since 1969 (minimum 10 games), per ESPN Research. And his player efficiency rating dropped from 26.1 in the regular season (sixth best in the NBA) to a below-average 13.8 in the playoffs. That's also the biggest drop for an All-Star in playoff history. For a player of that caliber, $40 million per year seems like an overpay. That uncertainty following his playoff shortcoming makes this deal a clear choice for Duren, even if he waited until the restricted free agency qualifying offer deadline to sign it. According to ESPN's Bobby Marks, even if Duren had received a max contract next summer after playing on the one-year qualifying offer in 2026-27, he would have received a maximum of $198.8 million over the next five years. This way, Duren locks in slightly more guaranteed money, and crucially, he locks it in now , as opposed to having to wait a year to ensure that he stayed healthy and played well enough to secure a max offer. That's a big win for Duren, as long as he's able to put any bad feelings engendered by the lengthy negotiating process behind him. Yet it's also a win for the Pistons, despite the hefty price tag. Duren is still only 22 years old, and he's already an All-NBA-level center with room for growth. His playoff struggles came under a bright spotlight, but it's worth remembering that they came in only 14 games -- a much smaller sample than the 70 excellent games he played in the regular season. Granted, Duren comes with some positional limitations, having never made a 3-pointer in his NBA career, which complicates his fit with fellow Pistons cornerstone Ausar Thompson . But Duren has the potential to develop into one of the NBA's elite screeners -- the Cunningham-Duren pick-and-roll was the most frequent partnership in the NBA last season -- and his size and mobility give him considerable untapped defensive potential. He might not be a superstar hub like Nikola Jokic or Victor Wembanyama , but centers with Duren's size and skill set are still quite rare. And after all the protracted rumors and drama, now he's right where he should be: teaming up with Cunningham for another half-decade to attempt to push the Pistons to even greater heights. Sept 25: Curry agrees to two-year extension Stephen Curry terms: Two years, $116 million (player option in year two) Grade: B "I'll make the decision when I'm ready," Curry told ESPN's Anthony Slater earlier this week, about his timeline for signing a new contract extension. Evidently, Curry didn't take much longer to get ready. Curry's new contract is a win for the Golden State Warriors in two ways. First, it locks up the Warriors legend for an extra two years, as he was poised to enter free agency next summer without a new deal. Second, he's taking a pay cut and signing for $20 million less than his maximum allowed amount, which could be crucial for a team that's trying to add -- and afford -- more star power next to him. For the moment, Curry's new deal keeps max cap space open for the Warriors next summer. However, that theoretical figure doesn't include Brandin Podziemski 's cap hold, Kristaps Porzingis ' mostly nonguaranteed contract, or extensions for Jimmy Butler III and Draymond Green , who are both free agents after this season. In that sense, a larger pay cut for Curry -- more akin to the two-year, $90 million deal Kevin Durant signed with the Houston Rockets last year -- would have been even better for the Warriors. But it's difficult to fault Curry for not taking so drastic a diminishment when he remains the Warriors' best player, even in his late 30s, and an extra $10 million per season is still beneficial for Golden State. The one real concern about this extension from the Warriors' side is whether Curry will still be worth roughly a third of the salary cap as he approaches his 40th birthday. He remains a singular offensive force when he's on the court, even if he's no longer producing like he did at his peak. Yet the injuries are mounting. Curry played just 43 games last season, and he has reached 65 games -- the threshold for many major award consideration -- just twice since 2018-19. Those two seasons came in 2023-24 and 2024-25, to be fair, so he has a recent history of health. But players typically don't become more available as they age, so it's worth wondering whether Curry's half-season absence last year is an unfortunate omen. However, if Curry does get hurt again, the Warriors almost certainly aren't winning much anyway; their potential success rests on his availability and production, first and foremost. So it's a fair bet for Golden State to bank on Curry's health and try to use its newfound extra cap space to surround him with the proper supporting cast. Sept. 22: Leonard, Raptors agree to $115 million extension Kawhi Leonard terms: Two years, $115 million, with player option in second year Grade: B- An extension agreement between Leonard and the Raptors seemed like a fait accompli as early as June, when the Raptors and Clippers first agreed on the terms of Leonard's eventual trade to Toronto. Leonard was set to enter the final season of his controversial contract, and the Raptors wouldn't have wanted to trade multiple unprotected picks for a one-year rental. This new deal will pay Leonard about $11 million less than his possible maximum, per ESPN's Shams Charania, which is capped at two years because of the NBA's over-38 rule. Leonard, now 35, will turn 38 years old at the end of this extension. Just because an extension was expected, however, doesn't mean it's an incredible value for the team involved. Leonard now projects to have among the dozen highest cap hits in the league during this deal. And while he's also one of the dozen best players in the NBA if he's on the court -- and you can read about how optimistic I am about his fit in Toronto this upcoming season in my trade grade -- that's a major if for a player with his age and extensive injury history. For comparison, last summer, Kevin Durant signed a new two-year contract with the Rockets, but that $90 million pact came with considerably greater savings for Houston. Leonard's new contract does give Toronto some extra wiggle room compared to if he had taken the max, but not by nearly the same amount. Instead, Leonard's new deal seems more akin to the four-year, $273 million extension Donovan Mitchell signed this summer. Both deals were anticipated, given the stature the two stars hold in their respective franchises, but neither deal seems likely to age especially well. The Raptors and Cavaliers are both hoping that they win now, because these big new contracts could hamper their ability to win in the future. Sept. 21: Thompson gets five-year extension from Pistons Ausar Thompson terms: Five years, $155 million Grade: B- It's fitting that Thompson agreed to his rookie extension within a few hours of Keyonte George doing the same, because both players signed for nearly identical amounts even though they have polar opposite playing styles. While George, who inked a five-year, $157.5 million extension with the Jazz, is a budding offensive star who might be the worst defensive player in the league, Thompson is an offensive liability who might be the NBA's best perimeter defender. Thompson finished third in Defensive Player of the Year voting last season, behind only Victor Wembanyama and Chet Holmgren , as he led the league in steals and routinely locked up the opponents' top scorer. Largely because of his spectacular defensive prowess, the Pistons have been better with Thompson on the floor in every season of his career to date. The concerns about his future come on the other end, because his shooting form, which was never strong to begin with, has gone backward. Last season, Thompson made just seven total 3-pointers on 23% accuracy, counting both regular season and playoffs. Compared to his brother, Amen , who signed a five-year, $208 million extension earlier this offseason, Ausar has demonstrated less offensive potential. Amen isn't a 3-point marksman, either, but he at least improved to 78% at the free-throw line last season, suggesting untapped shooting potential, while Ausar made just 57% of his free throws. Amen has also been better than his brother at scoring on drives and handling the ball; there's a reason he averaged 18.3 PPG last season to Ausar's mere 9.9. That's not to say Ausar is completely unproductive; he's effective in transition and a solid offensive rebounder -- a must, given how often he hangs out near the basket -- and the Pistons have still been better with him on the court than off, even on the offensive end. Yet that considerable weakness will limit Thompson's long-term ceiling and potentially complicate Detroit's roster-building plans, which drops this extension's grade a couple notches. In the modern NBA, it's not easy to win with a perimeter player who's such a non-shooter, and Thompson's new contract brings into greater question Jalen Duren 's future in Detroit, as the All-Star center lingers in restricted free agency . Sept. 18: Heat give Larsson a new deal Pelle Larsson terms: Four years, $60 million, with a mutual option in the fourth year Grade: B At summer league in Las Vegas this year, I had a conversation with various NBA folks about the Miami Heat . We were talking about the Heat's lineup possibilities around Giannis Antetokounmpo and how they might build a winner with depleted depth. One clear conclusion from this conversation was that Pelle Larsson was going to get a lot of minutes because Heat coach Erik Spoelstra adores him. The 25-year-old Swedish guard was a steal at the No. 44 pick in the 2024 draft, and he took a big step forward last season, averaging 11.4 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.4 assists. The Heat also trust him as a lead defender on the perimeter. He ranked fourth on the team in starts and fifth in total minutes last season. Larsson profiles as a high-floor, low-ceiling player, given his age and skill set. Most prominently, a shaky 3-point shot (33% in his career) means he's not truly a 3-and-D player but rather a jack of all trades who fits the Heat's preferred ethos with his hustle and stamina. Still, that high floor means a $15 million average for Larsson is a reasonable value for Miami, and this new deal will carry him through most of his prime years. Larsson must be happy with his new deal, given that his rookie contract was worth only $5.4 million over three years. Spoelstra must be happy to lock up one of his favorite players for the long term, too. Sept. 18: George, Jazz agree to extension Keyonte George terms: Five years, $157.5 million Grade: C+ George was one of the breakout players of the 2025-26 season, averaging 23.6 points and 6.1 assists while making 37% of his 3-pointers. He also boosted his efficiency from 7-8% below average in his first two seasons to 5% above average last year, which made him one of the top offensive guards in the sport. On its own, that trajectory -- combined with George's age, as he'll turn 23 in November -- makes him more than worthy of this new rookie extension, which will pay him an average of $31.5 million per year. For context, this contract will pay nearly $100 million less over half a decade compared with the possible 25% max (which Victor Wembanyama , another member of the 2023 draft class, signed earlier this offseason). But the complication with analyzing George's new deal is uncertainty about his ability on the other end. The Jazz have been worse with George on the floor versus when he's off in every season of his career to date. The defensive swing has been particularly problematic: Per Cleaning the Glass, Utah's defensive rating was 6.7 points worse with George last season and 8.7 points worse in 2024-25. Both marks ranked in the bottom 10% of players leaguewide. Because of that track record, advanced stats that factor in on/off data are much lower in their assessment of George than his shiny box score stats would suggest. DARKO rates George as the third-least-valuable defender in the league, and both estimated plus-minus and xRAPM put him all the way in last place. Other players in his range include the likes of Cam Thomas and Trae Young , who have proved difficult to build around because of their limitations. It's possible that this indictment of George is attributable to Utah's noncompetitive status during his time there; the Jazz haven't exactly been concerned about finishing 30th, 29th and 29th on defense over the past three years, as they've sought high draft picks instead of regular-season wins. Perhaps in a more competitive situation going forward, George will prove himself a mediocre or even normally below-average defender, rather than the truly terrible defender that his current metrics suggest. But it's impossible to know that yet, so this grade comes in lower than what might be expected for a rising young star signing a reasonable-looking contract. The other young guards in his new salary range are Immanuel Quickley and Jalen Suggs , whose contracts don't look like bargains a couple of years after they signed. George might be a better player than them, but it would have been nice to see his development, particularly on defense, for another year before judging his pricey new deal an unreserved win for the Jazz. Sept. 17: Bey signs extension with Pelicans Saddiq Bey terms: Three years, $55.5 million Grade: B Bey arrived in New Orleans as an afterthought. The former Detroit Piston , Atlanta Hawk and Washington Wizard missed the 2024-25 season because of a torn ACL before shipping to New Orleans in the Jordan Poole - CJ McCollum swap. Bey responded to his new circumstances with the best season of his career. He started 64 games (out of 72 total played) last season and averaged a career-high 17.7 points. He made 37% of his 3s and showed improvement as a perimeter defender. So the Pelicans gave him a big raise, from $6.6 million in this upcoming season to an average of $18.5 million over the following three years, which will keep Bey in New Orleans through his age-30 season. That's a solid contract for a solid player. It's a bit less clear how New Orleans plans to structure its wing rotation in the short and long term, with Bey, Bennedict Mathurin , Trey Murphy III and Herbert Jones all worthy of playing time, to say nothing of Zion Williamson and/or Derik Queen grabbing minutes at power forward. To that end, it's possible that Bey's new contract could make New Orleans more amenable to a trade of Murphy or Jones, two more established wings who could fetch draft picks from contenders. Sept 3: Rockets, Amen Thompson agree to five-year deal Amen Thompson terms: Five years, $208 million Grade: A- Thompson is the second member of the 2023 draft class to sign a rookie extension this summer, following in the steps of No. 1 pick Victor Wembanyama . That order tracks, as Thompson is the second-best player from that draft class after Wembanyama. He might not have exploded into superstardom as some expected -- and as Wembanyama did -- last season, but Thompson still fits the profile of a future two-way star. He's only 23 years old, he's one of the NBA's fiercest perimeter defenders and he boosted both his points (18.3 per game) and assists (5.3 per game) last season while leading the NBA in minutes played. Thompson's 3-point shot remains a glaring hole in his game, as he's at just 22% from distance in his career on low volume. That weakness could limit his ultimate upside, as he might be best suited as an ace defender and offensive role player, rather than a No. 1 scoring option. But given his present ability and future potential, extending him was a no-brainer for Houston. And as they have with other recent first-round picks, including Jabari Smith Jr ., Alperen Sengun and the since-traded Jalen Green , the Rockets actually negotiated with Thompson to save some money, rather than simply presenting him with a max deal to sign. Compare Thompson's new deal to Wembanyama's max contract, which is worth an estimated $252 million. The difference between the two extensions comes out to about $44 million over five years, or $8 million to $9 million per year -- which the Rockets can instead use to add an extra role player or help squeeze in other expensive players under the various tax thresholds. Locking in that number for Thompson now also means the Rockets won't run the risk of paying even more for his new deal if he makes an All-NBA team (or wins Defensive Player of the Year or MVP) this upcoming season, which would have allowed him to qualify for rookie supermax status. This deal thus carries tremendous benefits for both parties. Thompson gains generational wealth before he reaches his mid-20s, and the Rockets both retain their most talented young player for the long term and maintain a bit of financial flexibility in the process. That sounds like a win-win. Aug. 26: Kuminga, Timberwolves agree on two-year deal Jonathan Kuminga terms: Two years, $12.4 million, player option in Year 2 Grade: A- Few players in recent memory have received more fanfare, relative to their on-court impact, than Kuminga. The former No. 7 pick was a key member of the Warriors' theoretical " two timelines " dynastic extension, and he was a main character of the 2025 offseason, as he lingered in restricted free agency. A year later, however, Kuminga's new contract actually deserves the attention -- but more for the context of his new situation than because of his own development. One of the main reasons that I was critical of the Timberwolves' trade for LaMelo Ball is that the series of transactions they used to acquire the All-Star point guard left them with a giant, gaping hole at power forward. They were already a top-heavy team without much depth, and then they parted with Julius Randle and Naz Reid in the process. And with the LeBron James dream dashed last month , the Timberwolves had few remaining resources to acquire another frontcourt contributor. The Ball trade left them with almost no draft capital -- they have zero tradeable first-round picks, and their only tradeable second is a top-50-protected selection from Memphis in 2030 -- and they're hard-capped at the second apron, with only about $4 million in wiggle room below that barrier. (Thus, they will have to figure out a way to dump some salary before officially signing Kuminga.) So given all those limitations, and the slim pickings nearly two months into free agency, Kuminga was clearly the best option available. The expectation is that he'll join Ball, Anthony Edwards , Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert in a talented starting lineup, where Kuminga's ability to run the floor should get him enough easy buckets every game to keep his scoring average in double figures. Kuminga isn't a perfect fit in his new role. His outside shooting struggles (33% on 3s in his career) could strain his partnership with Gobert on offense, and it's still an open question whether Kuminga will ever bring the consistency required of a nailed-down NBA starter. He has always shown flashes, but never for more than a few games or weeks at a time. Yet on the other hand, Kuminga is still just 24 years old, and he clearly has potential if he can find the right situation in which to thrive; most recently, he was one of Atlanta's best players in the playoffs. According to ESPN's Shams Charania, other teams were interested in signing Kuminga to a larger contract this summer, which points to his continued desirability despite his flaws. He doesn't need to be a star in Minnesota, either, but rather a competent role player. He may not even close games for his new team, whose five best players are probably Gobert, McDaniels and a trio of guards. But what the Timberwolves needed most of all was a capable power forward who can protect McDaniels -- one of the league's best perimeter defenders -- from sliding up to that position full time. They found one, at a reasonable price. As long as Kuminga stays healthy -- he has appeared in only 83 combined games over the past two seasons -- and engaged, he'll provide a meaningful upgrade to a fringe title contender next season. Aug. 26: Pels, Mathurin reach two-year deal Bennedict Mathurin terms: Two years, $16 million, player option in second year Grade: B+ The Pelicans are finally getting involved in the summer transaction cycle, after essentially sitting on their hands for the first two months of the offseason. They picked their first spot well. Mathurin is still just 24 years old, with the potential befitting a former No. 6 pick. He's a strong individual scorer who averaged a career-high 17.6 PPG last year, and his driving ability and free throw generation remain standout skills. Among all active non-centers with at least 5,000 career minutes, Mathurin ranks sixth in career free throw attempt rate (or the number of free throw attempts per field goal attempt). The rest of the top 10 is filled with superstars: That said, Mathurin has been a one-dimensional player throughout his career, which holds him back from reaching the same overall level as those superstars. He has averaged only 1.9 assists per game, and he's a weak defender despite his 6-foot-5 frame. It's notable that both the Pacers -- who saw Mathurin up close for four years -- and Clippers, who had him for half a season after the Ivica Zubac trade, were comfortable letting him go despite his youth and potential, and that Mathurin didn't attract other suitors as a restricted free agent. But for this price and contract length, Mathurin's addition is a low-risk gamble for New Orleans, which is in need of more talent. (Expect further transactions before the season begins to create more space to fit Mathurin below the first apron.) The second-year player option reduces some of the upside for the Pelicans, as they could lose Mathurin as early as next summer if he takes a leap under their purview. But they'd surely be thrilled if he made that leap in the first place. Aug. 21: Thompson to join Heat after Mavs buyout Klay Thompson terms: Two years, $13 million, player option in second year Grade: B- Thompson's on-court value no longer matches his name value, as a future Hall of Famer who was a centerpiece of the NBA's last great dynasty. There's a reason, after all, that the Mavericks were amenable to buying Thompson out of the last year of his contract to pave his path to Miami. He is now 36 years old and nowhere near the sort of two-way star he was at his peak. Instead, the five-time All-Star is now a well below-average player. DARKO Career DPM Progression But Thompson will bring one important skill to Miami that the Heat are currently lacking: Even as he has declined, he has remained an elite shooter. Thompson has made at least 38% of his 3-pointers on high volume in every season of his career, and even coming off the bench last season, he ranked among the top 20 players in made 3s per game. Incidentally, Thompson ranked second in total 3s from a reserve last season -- one spot behind Tim Hardaway Jr ., his new teammate on Miami's perimeter. Because the Heat already added Hardaway in free agency , it's possible that Thompson's presence will be redundant. And a two-year, $13 million deal with a second-year player option is less of an obvious win for Miami than a veteran minimum would have been. But in truth, the Heat need all the shooting they can get around Giannis Antetokounmpo , after they lost Norman Powell and Tyler Herro , their top two shooters last season. And if any team can cover for Thompson on the defensive end, where he's now a liability because of his age and injury history, it might be a group with Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo , Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins , to say nothing of Erik Spoelstra pulling the strategic strings. It's still unlikely that Thompson, at this stage of his career, will be a major difference-maker for his new team. But Thompson is a better use of a roster spot than other options Miami had to complete its 2026-27 rotation. Aug. 21: DeRozan joins Nuggets on one-year deal DeMar DeRozan terms: One year, $3.9 million Grade: B Presumably, DeRozan signed this contract knowing he'd likely be asked to come off the bench in Denver, even though he has started every NBA game he has played since his rookie year -- 1,250 and counting, between the regular season and playoffs. That shift couldn't come at a better time for the Nuggets, whose bench was incredibly depleted following the Peyton Watson sign-and-trade earlier this week. This is far from a like-for-like replacement, to be clear: DeRozan is about as different from Watson as two similarly sized players can be. The 23-year-old Watson is strongest on defense and -- in a new turn -- from the 3-point line; the 37-year-old DeRozan is a midrange master with considerable defensive limitations. That difference could make DeRozan a somewhat clunky fit in Denver, where he won't patch the defensive holes left by Watson's departure, and where his lack of 3-point range could complicate his fit with Nikola Jokic (and Christian Braun , if he can't rebound from last season's 30% performance from distance). But on a relative basis, DeRozan should provide a major upgrade in his new home. Until the six-time All-Star joined on a veteran minimum contract, the Nuggets' highest-scoring reserves were projected as backup center Marvin Bagley III (10.5 points per game last season) and wing Julian Strawther (7.2). Even in his late 30s, DeRozan offers a different level of scoring and playmaking -- he's a very underrated passer -- than any other option outside the Nuggets' starting lineup. He should be able to help stabilize the offense when Jokic or Jamal Murray rest, as he has continued to score efficiently even in a dour situation in Sacramento over the past two seasons. For years now, Denver's bench has been a problem, and DeRozan won't come close to solving that issue all on his own. But it's slightly less of an issue today than it was yesterday. Aug. 20: Harden, Cavs agree to new contract James Harden terms: Three years, $97 million, with a player option in the third year Grade: B At this point, you know what you're getting with Harden. He has remained a metronomic offensive force even into his late 30s; he can create for others and score of his own accord inside, outside and at the free throw line. He also rarely misses time, as he has appeared in 70 or more games in each of the past three seasons. That combination makes for a powerful regular-season catalyst. In 15 of his 17 NBA seasons, including each of the last 10, Harden has finished the year with a team that won at least 50 games (or the equivalent winning percentage in a shortened season). He has never finished with a losing record. You also know, however, the downsides that come with relying on Harden. He was a relatively indifferent defender even in his 20s, and now he's one of the least active defenders in the league. His production also routinely shrinks in the postseason, or at the very least becomes wildly inconsistent. Those attributes are essentially baked into Harden's player profile at this point, and his return to Cleveland also seemed baked in as soon as the Cavaliers traded Darius Garland for him at last season's deadline . The Clippers weren't willing to extend Harden at his desired amount, so he sought a trade to a team that would. And after Harden declined his $42 million player option earlier this summer, it was only a matter of time before the Cavaliers completed the rest of their offseason business -- which they did with the Peyton Watson sign-and-trade on Wednesday -- and brought back Harden on a longer-term deal with a lower annual value. The resulting contract is a year longer than would be optimal for the Cavaliers, as it gives Harden a player option in his age-39 season. A straight two-year deal in the $60 million range would have protected Cleveland more against potential decline as Harden ages. But for all the holes in Harden's game, he's still a valuable playmaker and regular-season innings eater, and his backcourt partnership with Donovan Mitchell worked reasonably well in limited time last year. The Cavaliers certainly couldn't afford to lose him, with Garland already gone and no means to replace his production with another trade or free agent signing. That 2028-29 player option could -- and likely will -- prove problematic in a couple of years. But the Cavaliers are an all-in, win-now team, and they're hoping that Harden helps them finally get over the playoff hump and return to the Finals at some point before then. Aug. 13: Beal re-signs with Clippers Bradley Beal terms: Two years, $13.2 million Grade: C Beal declined a $5.6 million player option in late June before agreeing to a new deal with the LA Clippers six weeks later. He didn't make much of an impression in his first stint in Los Angeles, appearing in only six games before undergoing season-ending hip surgery . In those six games, Beal averaged a career-low 8.2 points and experienced a startling decline in efficiency and production. His player efficiency rating ranked 498th out of 503 players with at least 100 minutes played last season. On the one hand, it would be easy to chalk up that decline to Beal's injury and expect a bounce-back performance in 2026-27. On the other hand, Beal is now 33 years old with a fairly extensive injury history -- he hasn't played more than 53 games since 2020-21 with the Washington Wizards -- and he was already on the downslope of his career in Phoenix before becoming a Clipper. Because of that context, it's hard to expect much of anything from Beal at this point. His re-signing won't complicate the Clippers' finances, but it likely won't move the needle on the court, either. Aug. 6: Suns sign Brooks to extension through 2030 Dillon Brooks terms: Three years, $73 million Grade: B- Brooks was a revelation in his first season in Phoenix, after heading to the Suns in the trade that sent Kevin Durant to Houston. Not only did the veteran wing average a career-high 20.2 points per game, but his attitude and mentality spread throughout the franchise. "He's exactly the type of player [who fits] what we talk about here in Phoenix, what we want to be, the identity of the Suns," team owner Mat Ishbia told ESPN's Tim MacMahon earlier this year. Phoenix is keeping him around for a few years longer, at a fairly reasonable price. Brooks is entering the last year of a four-year, $86 million contract that accounted for about 15% of the salary cap per season; his new three-year extension projects to make up about 13% of the salary cap each season until 2029-30. From the pure perspective of his on-court value, Brooks doesn't project to be worth that much money, given his age -- this extension covers his age-32 to 34 seasons, when he'll likely be in the decline phase -- and unimpressive advanced statistics. He has never been an efficient scorer, with a below-average true shooting mark in every season of his career. But given his cultural fit and leadership responsibilities in Phoenix -- and the fact that the rising salary cap means a $24.3 million average salary will account for such a manageable portion of it -- this extension makes a lot of sense for the Suns. It's not as team-friendly as some of Phoenix's other deals this summer, such as bringing back Collin Gillespie and Jordan Goodwin , but it might have a greater impact nonetheless because of Brooks' more prominent role on the team. Aug. 2: Marshall, Mavericks agree to extension Naji Marshall terms: Three years, $52.2 million Grade: B- Marshall was set to enter unrestricted free agency next summer but instead signed a three-year contract that will keep him with the Dallas Mavericks through the 2029-30 season. Not accounting for inflation, this extension is essentially double what he signed for two years ago, when he joined the Mavericks on a three-year, $27 million free agent contract. He has earned a raise in that time. In his first four seasons, all with the Pelicans, Marshall never averaged more than 9.1 points, but he has averaged 13.2 and 15.2 points in his two seasons in Dallas. Marshall's rise has gone under the radar amid all the other drama surrounding the Mavericks during those years, but he has quietly blossomed into a solid NBA forward. After that developmental leap, Marshall grades out an average player -- he scores with near-average efficiency on a near-average usage rate (20.3% in Dallas, versus an average of 20.0%), leading to a near-average player efficiency rating (15.3 in Dallas, versus an average of 15.0). So why does an extension that will keep that caliber of player in town through the rest of his prime, for only around 10% of the salary cap, receive a mere B-minus grade rather than higher marks? Because of one key weakness in Marshall's game: He's only a 30% career 3-point shooter, and he has been even worse (28%) in Dallas. Granted, Marshall has enjoyed considerable improvement from 2-point range, and a healthy free throw rate buoys his overall efficiency. But absent a better 3-point shot, he won't fulfill the ultimate 3-and-D potential. If he had a more threatening jump shot, Marshall would be a surefire starter, but he's instead stuck with the profile of a fringe starter or solid bench player for a good team. That weakness also complicates his fit on a Mavericks roster with so many other questionable shooters in the frontcourt, from Cooper Flagg to 2026 lottery pick Morez Johnson Jr . to a host of paint-bound centers. Because of its length and manageable cap figure, the Mavericks are unlikely to ever seriously regret giving Marshall this extension. But they're also unlikely to end up viewing it as a slam dunk success, either. July 28: Draymond back to Warriors Draymond Green terms: One year, $27.7 million Grade: C Before the offseason began, the expectation was that Green would play out the 2026-27 season on a $27.7 million deal. He had a player option for that amount and likely wouldn't have received any more on the open market as a 36-year-old with more value to the Golden State Warriors than any other team. That expectation changed for about a month, after Green declined his player option to give the Warriors the financial flexibility to pursue free agent LeBron James . But after James went to Philadelphia 76ers rather than northern California, it made sense for Green to re-sign with the Warriors for the same one-year deal he declined a month earlier. Because the baseline for these free agent grades is a "C," and because Green stuck with the baseline expectation entering this summer, that's the logical grade to give this deal. But the one-year pact, rather than a multiyear deal with a lower annual value but more total guaranteed money, sets up a fascinating situation next summer. Golden State's three highest-paid players -- Stephen Curry , Jimmy Butler III and Green -- could all enter free agency in 2027, while the fourth-highest-paid player is Kristaps Porzingis , whose deal is guaranteed for only $3 million in 2027-28. That means Golden State could set itself up for tremendous cap space a year from now. Even a hefty new deal for Curry, who becomes extension-eligible on Aug. 29, wouldn't take up all that space. More on the Warriors' offseason July 24: LeBron chooses 76ers LeBron James terms: Two years, $8 million Grade: A+ How James fits in a new-look, star-studded lineup in Philadelphia, immediately becomes one of the most fascinating questions in the NBA. On the one hand, James averaged 20.9 points per game last season, tied with his rookie campaign for the lowest of his career. His 27% usage rate was his lowest ever, and his time of possession was by far his lowest in the tracking era (since 2013-14): James handled the ball for 3.8 minutes per game in 2025-26, a 37% drop from his previous low of 5.3 minutes. He also averaged just 15.5 picks per 100 possessions as the ball handler, a 40% drop from his previous low. Yet on the other hand, James was still productive and efficient by any measure, and he settled much more comfortably into a secondary offensive role -- which he'll presumably occupy once more in Philadelphia -- as the season continued. His 59% true shooting was right in line with his career average (also 59%) and his mark across eight seasons with the Lakers (60%). And he averaged 7.2 assists per game, generated gobs of free throws and played 1,989 minutes, which was the third most on the Lakers. Full deal grades, winners and losers July 11: Bucks bring back Trent on big deal Gary Trent Jr . terms : Four years, $64 million Grade: D- Half a decade ago, Trent signed a three-year, $54 million contract with Toronto. It made sense at the time: Trent was 22 years old and coming off a breakout season, during which he was traded for Norman Powell . He looked like a strong 3-and-D prospect. On Saturday, Trent agreed to similar terms on a new deal: four years, $64 million to stay with the Bucks. But there's only one problem: He has declined significantly since his early 20s. Trent was arguably the least valuable veteran rotation player in the entire NBA last season. He averaged only 8.1 points, 1.2 assists and 1.0 rebounds per game, and his 3-point percentage fell to a league-average 36%. Out of 279 players with at least 1,000 minutes, Trent ranked 276th in both box plus/minus and player efficiency rating, and every player below him was 21 or younger. Trent, conversely, was an eight-year veteran in his age-27 season. Given the combination of that decline and the Bucks' overabundance of young guards who need playing time -- after the draft and the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade -- it makes little sense for Milwaukee to lavish Trent with a new contract with so many dollars and so many years. Still in his 20s, he has time to bounce back, but for the moment, he profiles more like a minimum-salary player than one who deserves eight figures per year. Coincidentally, Trent played on minimum or near-minimum deals for Milwaukee in each of the past two seasons, despite coming off much better performances in both years. Last summer, he signed a two year, $7.5 million deal with a second-year player option, which he declined, despite his woeful 2025-26 campaign, to secure a much larger payday this summer. July 10: Wemby, Spurs agree on rookie extension Victor Wembanyama terms: Five years, $252 million Grade: A+ This might be the easiest transaction I'll ever grade. Before last season, 83% of the NBA's general managers chose Wembanyama as the player they'd most like to build a franchise around. And that number has probably risen since, as Wembanyama was the unanimous Defensive Player of the Year , finished third in MVP voting and was the best player on a Finals team in 2025-26. The Spurs would have received an "A" grade for extending Wembanyama no matter the contract details. He could have received the max, a player option and "Rose rule" salary escalator language, and Spurs brass would have been thrilled. But in the end, he did not take every possible bell and whistle allowed for a player of his experience level, which boosts this grade to an "A+" for the Spurs. According to ESPN's Shams Charania, Wembanyama is locking himself into a 25% maximum contract. He could have chosen an extension that would rise to 30% of the cap if he received postseason honors next year -- which seems like a virtual lock if Wembanyama reaches the 65-game minimum for awards consideration again. Many other young stars have opted for that latter route in recent years, and they deserve no blame for maximizing their earnings. Evan Mobley , for instance, landed a 30% supermax before winning Defensive Player of the Year in 2025. But Wembanyama has evidently taken a lesson from the star guard who beat the Spurs in the Finals last month, after the Knicks' title run was aided in part by Jalen Brunson's decision to sacrifice some of his own potential earnings to help New York build a championship roster. The difference between 25% and 30% of the cap projects as $8.7 million next season, per ESPN's Bobby Marks, and that gap would grow over the course of Wembanyama's extension to a total of $50 million over five years. Now, the Spurs can use those savings to extend Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper , and still bolster the rotation around those young stars. July 8: Post to join Grizzlies on offer sheet Quinten Post terms: Three years, $30 million Grade: B- Post made a little bit of history with this contract, as the Warriors chose not to match Memphis's offer sheet to retain their 7-footer. It represents the first time a restricted free agent's original team didn't match an offer sheet since 2020, when Bogdan Bogdanovic left the Kings for the Hawks, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks. That decision made sense for Golden State. Post is far younger than Al Horford and Kristaps Porzingis , but his stretch big skill set is duplicative next to those veteran spacers. And more importantly, this level of financial commitment would have been punishing for the Warriors, who are hard-capped at the first apron and still have a fair bit of summer business -- re-signing Draymond Green and potentially adding LeBron James -- to accomplish before reaching that barrier. For the Grizzlies, however, fitting Post into their cap sheet is a relatively easy feat after they traded the more expensive Santi Aldama . Post, 26, is a lesser version of Aldama on offense but a superior defender; opponents have made 58% of their shots at the rim against Post in his career, per NBA Advanced Stats, which is a solid number for a reserve big. Whether Post is actually a formidable stretch big is a more worrying question for Memphis, as his 3-point accuracy fell from 41% in his rookie season to just 34% last year. And with Zach Edey and the recently acquired Isaiah Stewart also on the roster, to say nothing of No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer and the recently acquired Jerami Grant and Taylor Hendricks , Memphis is chock-full of players who are best suited to play the 4 and 5. Post brings a unique element in that group because of his combination of size and shooting. But if Edey can stay on the court next season, it's unclear how much Post will actually play. July 7: Mitchell, Cavaliers agree to four-year deal Donovan Mitchell terms : Four years, $273 million Grade : B- Mitchell is a consistently excellent NBA superstar. He has been an All-Star in each of the past seven seasons and a first- or second-team All-NBA honoree in three of his four years in Cleveland. The Cavaliers gave up a haul in their blockbuster trade for Mitchell in 2022, and they have to be mostly pleased with the results. Even if they haven't reached the Finals with Mitchell, they've been a consistent contender with him aboard. And with Darius Garland now traded, James Harden well past his prime and Evan Mobley stuck on a developmental plateau, Mitchell remains the team's clear No. 1 option even as he approaches his 30th birthday. With two seasons left on his current contract, including a player option in 2027-28, there was an imperative for Cleveland to extend Mitchell now, lest he decline his option and leave in free agency next summer. But that logistical reality doesn't make this new contract any more comfortable for Cleveland. Mitchell's maximum extension will start at $60.9 million in 2027-28, per ESPN's Bobby Marks, and will run through his age-34 season in 2030-31, when he'd be projected to hold a player option for $75.5 million. This extension is a gamble that Mitchell will enjoy an elongated prime, but that's a risky proposition. He's a relatively small guard who regularly misses time each season, though he admittedly hasn't suffered any severe injuries; he's played between 53 and 71 games every year since 2018-19. He also seems to wear down by the postseason and struggles to maintain his form when the games matter most. Mitchell famously reached the conference finals for the first time this spring, but he was far from his best self -- his true shooting fell from 61% in the regular season to 56% in the playoffs -- along the way. Devoting such a high percentage of the salary cap to a second-tier star -- someone who makes All-NBA teams but never seriously contends for MVP -- complicates a team's roster-building options in the NBA's current financial environment. In a world in which the Celtics struggled to find any trade partners for Jaylen Brown , who's owed an average of $61.7 million over the next three seasons, a new contract for Mitchell at an average of $68.2 million per season is similarly daunting. Cleveland's new pact with Mitchell is similar to the Suns' deal with Devin Booker , who signed an extension last summer that will pay him an estimated $68.8 million in his age-33 season in 2029-30. Mitchell has experienced higher highs than Booker, who has been a top-10 player (in All-NBA terms) only once. But they're in the same broad category of star guards who probably can't be the best player on a championship team. That probably qualifier is important, because Jalen Brunson just provided proof of concept for a small scoring guard to win Finals MVP. The Cavaliers hope Mitchell can pull off the same feat at some point during the span of his new contract -- preferably on the earlier side, before he reaches his mid-30s with an escalating salary. But Mitchell is a rung below Brunson in terms of postseason pedigree, and, crucially, Brunson signed a below-market extension to help New York construct a robust roster around him. Mitchell doesn't deserve any blame for not taking as much money as he could -- but the fact of the matter is that his new extension, combined with Cleveland's already-limited resources, won't make it any easier for the Cavaliers to improve in the near future, when they most need that improvement to take advantage of Mitchell's remaining prime. July 5: Hachimura, Clippers agree to two-year deal Rui Hachimura terms: Two years, $28 million Grade: B+ Hachimura's $14 million per year places him in the middle of several other power forward types who have signed in free agency this summer: John Collins at $17 million annually, Tobias Harris at $15.5 million and Sandro Mamukelashvili at $13 million. Compared with that group, Hachimura has the best singular standout skill. After a poor start to his career from long range, Hachimura has developed into an excellent shooter. Over his three full seasons with the Lakers, he made 42.6% of his 3-pointers, which ranked second (behind Luke Kennard ) out of 216 players with at least 500 attempts in that span. The rest of Hachimura's game isn't so special, which is why he's not at the top end of the power forward market. He's a sturdy defender because of his size (6-foot-8, 230 pounds), but not a game changer on that end of the floor, and he has never created many shots for others (0.8 assists per game last season, 1.2 per game in his career). For the Clippers, Hachimura represents a low-risk floor-raiser after the team turned over its entire roster over the past few years. And while Hachimura might have made more sense for a contender, where his shooting could have made a real difference as a supplement to stars -- as it did with the Lakers during their conference finals run in 2023 -- he preferred to stay in Los Angeles, per ESPN's Shams Charania. That sounds like a win-win deal. July 3: Drummond to Knicks as champs find a center Andre Drummond terms: One year, $3.9 million Grade: B- Stylistically, the Knicks couldn't have found a better replacement for Mitchell Robinson . He and Drummond are massive centers, indefatigable rebounders and poor free throw shooters. Robinson is the best offensive rebounder in the NBA, but so too was Drummond, once upon a time. He led the league in offensive boards per game from 2013-14 through 2019-20, and his per-36 numbers remain similar to this day. When Drummond enters games, he'll give the Knicks this same offensive advantage that Robinson did. But this is a qualitative downgrade for the Knicks. There's a reason that Robinson commanded a $47.4 million contract over three years, while Drummond signed for the veteran minimum. Notably, Drummond is a worse defender. He allowed opponents to shoot 68% at the rim last season, one of the worst marks for a center, while Robinson was at 58%. That difference could be an issue in the playoffs, where such weaknesses are magnified and Drummond hasn't had much success; he won the first series of his career this spring, when the Philadelphia 76ers upset the Boston Celtics . If the Knicks were never going to go into the second apron for any reason, as owner James Dolan suggested , then they couldn't have afforded to retain Robinson. Drummond is a worthy replacement in that context. But if Karl-Anthony Towns is in foul trouble in a crucial moment next postseason and the Knicks have Drummond playing big minutes, New York might regret this financially motivated roster change. July 3: Queta returns to Boston on four-year deal Neemias Queta terms: Four years, $56 million Grade: A- The same advanced stats that have so riled up Celtics fans in recent weeks due to their mild skepticism of Jaylen Brown positively adore Queta. xRAPM ranks Queta in the 96th percentile of players in per-possession impact, and estimated plus-minus ranks him in the 95th percentile. That's pretty good for a former two-way player who had never reached 1,000 minutes in a season before 2025-26. But Queta was extraordinary stepping into Boston's vacated starting center role, averaging 10.2 points, 8.4 rebounds and 2.1 stocks (steals plus blocks) per game. Most importantly, the Celtics had a plus-13.2 net rating with him on the floor, the highest mark on the team. The Celtics extended Queta for the long term with a two-step maneuver. First, they exercised his $2.7 million team option for 2026-27, giving the team extra financial flexibility for next season -- which they used to sign Mitchell Robinson , another center with excellent advanced stats. And second, they inked Queta to a four-year extension that will start in 2027-28, keeping him in Boston through his prime. Especially given other, more expensive contracts handed out to centers this offseason, Queta's new deal looks like a bargain for Boston, if his performance last season is any indication of the half-decade to come. Only two small nuggets of concern drop this grade from an A to an A-minus. First, Queta has a relatively short track record of that level of play. And second, he struggled in the postseason as Boston lost in seven games against Philadelphia. It remains to be seen whether Queta functions better as a regular-season innings-eater or a championship-level contributor. July 2: Eason, Rockets agree to five-year deal Tari Eason terms: Five years, $81.5 million Grade: A The NBA's current cap environment is designed to punish complacency. In previous eras, teams could prioritize good feelings and round up on their contract offers -- giving a slightly sub-max player the max, proposing an extra year or a player option, and so on. But not anymore. Now, every dollar beneath the apron counts, and flexibility is the new guiding light. Front offices must be cutthroat rather than complacent if they want to build a sustainable winning roster over the long term. It has taken some time to adapt to that new state of affairs, and even now, not every team has made the adjustment. But the Rockets have been one of the new model teams in how to negotiate with their own players: Kevin Durant , Alperen Sengun , Jalen Green and Fred VanVleet all signed deals with some team-friendly elements, rather than their individual maximums. They did it again with Eason, one of the best 3-and-D prospects in the league. The 6-foot-8 Eason is a phenomenal defender with positional versatility, and he and Amen Thompson -- who's eligible for a rookie contract extension of his own this summer -- could continue harassing opposing guards and wings for years to come. He has also improved on the offensive end, even if that will never be his greatest strength. Last season, Eason made a career-best 36% of his 3-pointers on a career-high number of attempts (though his 2-point percentage plummeted at the same time). Perhaps most importantly, Eason has been mostly healthy for two seasons in a row, which assuages the greatest concern about his profile: He played just 22 games in 2023-24, but he has increased his availability to 57 and 60 games over the last two seasons. At just over $16 million per year for a player with his skill set and potential, this could end up as one of the best value contracts signed by any player this summer. At the very least, a version of Eason who's locked in for half a decade at this price should be very attractive in a trade, if the Rockets ever decide to make him available in a deal for another star. And at the most, he'll deliver tremendous value to Houston over the course of this deal, as the Rockets use the added flexibility from their hard bargains to continue upgrading their roster and constructing a contender. July 2: Simons, 76ers agree on two-year deal Anfernee Simons terms: Two years, $12.3 million (player option in second year) Grade: C+ Simons is one of the NBA's premier microwave scorers, the spiritual heir to the likes of Lou Williams and Jamal Crawford. With the Celtics last season, he averaged 14.2 points in 24.5 minutes per game while making 39.5% of his 3-pointers, before a trade to Chicago and a wrist injury ended his season . He'll now serve as the 76ers' third guard, replacing the departed Quentin Grimes , who signed a much larger deal (four years, $60 million) with the Lakers. Equally capable of spotting up on the perimeter or running a pick-and-roll on his own, Simons should give Philadelphia instant offense off the bench. But this is a curious fit because of Simons' ineffectiveness on the other end. He's a small guard whom advanced stats rank as one of the NBA's worst defenders. So it's unclear whether he'll be able to play next to Tyrese Maxey without compromising Philadelphia's defense beyond repair. It's also unclear what Simons' arrival means for No. 22 pick Labaron Philon Jr. , another small guard with defensive question marks. Philon weighed 176 pounds at the NBA combine, which made him the lightest player taken in the first round. For that reason, it's difficult to imagine him and Simons playing together in bench units. Perhaps that doesn't matter much to the 76ers, who have more pressing win-now demands following the Jaylen Brown trade. It's unlikely that a rookie guard taken after the lottery will help a contender next year, anyway. But with Brown and VJ Edgecombe able to soak up much of the playmaking duties when Maxey goes to the bench, if Philadelphia staggers its best perimeter players, Simons seems like more of an oddly fitting luxury than a player who fills a glaring need. His signing brings the 76ers within $4 million of the first apron hard cap, and one wonders whether they could have found a more compelling use of their remaining space. July 1: Oubre joins Pacers on two-year deal Kelly Oubre Jr . terms: Two years, $17 million Grade: B No NBA team can have enough 3-and-D wings. That role is too valuable and too versatile. So, on the surface, adding Oubre to a group that already includes Aaron Nesmith , Andrew Nembhard and Ben Sheppard makes all the sense in the world. It is worth asking how many members of that group are actually reliable shooters. Nesmith is a given, at 39.6% from distance over four seasons in Indiana. But there's a curious trend with the other three members of Indiana's wing rotation. Oubre, Nembhard and Sheppard were all around 33% in their careers before last season, which is quite poor. But then they all improved to reach league-average accuracy. Oubre's jump was particularly notable because he had the greatest subpar track record heading into 2025-26; he shot a career-high 36% just one year after shooting 29% from distance. There's a potential downside here: If Oubre, Nembhard and Sheppard all regress to their career norms next season, Indiana's offense might not improve as much as expected with the return of Tyrese Haliburton because they'll miss a lot of 3s on kickout passes from their star point guard. But if the trio's league-average performance from distance is more than a one-year fluke, then Indiana might just have enough for a Finals return. July 1: Spurs sign wing Tobias Harris Tobias Harris terms: Two years, $31 million Grade: A- The Spurs had a number of mid-30s veterans on their roster last season, but they contributed much more off the court than via their actual play on it. Harrison Barnes played only 17 minutes in the Finals, and Bismack Biyombo , Kelly Olynyk and Mason Plumlee didn't play at all. So, San Antonio entered the offseason with two holes to fill: on-court veteran experience and a two-way power forward with more size than Julian Champagnie and more skill than Carter Bryant , after the likes of OG Anunoby and (briefly) Julius Randle presented problems in the postseason. Enter Tobias Harris. Harris will turn 34 later this month, and he has never made an All-Star team or received end-of-season awards votes of any kind. But he remains a well-above-average contributor because of his consistency and all-around play. Harris is almost always available, having appeared in at least 62 games in each of the past dozen seasons. He's a viable 3-point shooter (37% both in his career and last season) who can create his own shot in a pinch, and he's a solid rebounder and defender. Above all, Harris' teams have been better with him on the court in six of the past seven seasons, per Cleaning the Glass -- never by a gigantic amount but consistently enough to form a recognizable trend. Even at his age, that sort of production should be worth more than $15.5 million per season. It's possible that the Spurs could have found a superior free agent option for their midlevel exception; Rui Hachimura's shooting advantage over Harris could make him a better fit in San Antonio, for instance. But because the Spurs' contracts will grow much more expensive in the next few years, as their top-five picks start receiving extensions, they had an incentive to limit the years on their contracts this summer. And Harris' age evidently made him amenable to signing for just two years, even as other players in this range sign for longer (see, for instance, Sandro Mamukelashvili's and Dean Wade's four-year pacts with the Lakers and 76ers, respectively). By signing Harris at this price, the Spurs got better, and they got a bargain, simultaneously. July 1: Celtics sign former Knicks big Mitchell Robinson Mitchell Robinson terms: Three years, $47.4 million (player option in third year) Grade: B+ Boston likes to shoot 3-pointers, and Robinson has never even attempted -- let alone made -- a 3. But this signing is an example of the Celtics doubling down on a strength, regardless. With Neemias Queta replacing Al Horford and Kristaps Porzingis as the Celtics' primary center last season, they added a new wrinkle to their offense in an effort to win the possession battle. They ranked fifth in offensive rebounding rate, their first time in the top 10 under Joe Mazzulla. And it just so happens that Robinson is one of the best offensive rebounders in NBA history. Among players with at least 5,000 career minutes, Robinson is tied for second (with Dennis Rodman) in career offensive rebounding rate. That's just one of several fascinating elements to this signing, which sends a key player from the champs to one of their biggest rivals. This isn't a consideration notable enough to affect many free agent grades, but the fact that the Celtics not only added Robinson, but simultaneously took him away from the second-apron-averse New York Knicks adds to their score. Robinson is a unique player with both obvious strengths and just as obvious weaknesses. He'll offer Boston unparalleled second-chance opportunities, rim protection and much-needed above-the-rim athleticism, and he'll also frustrate Celtics fans with his free throw struggles and inconsistent availability. In games between the Celtics and Knicks, Mazzulla was one of the most frequent Hack-a-Mitch practitioners, as Robinson's woes at the charity stripe only grew more extreme. He made just 41% of his free throws in the 2025-26 regular season, and an even worse 29% in the playoffs. The Knicks' fear of Robinson free throws often kept him off the floor. So did various injuries, as Robinson's 60 games last season were his most since 2021-22; in the two previous years, he played just 48 regular-season games combined . But Boston has the depth to manage Robinson's minutes carefully throughout the regular season, and his new team is really hoping he raises its ceiling in the playoffs. Queta excelled in the starting lineup last season -- up until the playoffs, when he lost his way against Philadelphia. Robinson is an NBA champion who won't be cowed by the moment next spring. July 1: Warriors bring back De'Anthony Melton on 2-year deal De'Antony Melton terms: Two years, $11 million (player option in second year) Grade: A Last summer, Melton signed a two-year deal with the Warriors, with a player option in the second year. He opted out and is going the same route this summer, just with a slightly higher price tag following a strong comeback season from a torn ACL in November 2024. Regardless of whether the Warriors' star ambitions pan out this summer, Melton will be an excellent fit on their roster as a do-it-all guard with a knack for forcing turnovers. He doesn't need the ball to contribute, and if his 3-point shot bounces back with more time removed from his injury -- he was at 29% last season, a big step down from his previous 37% career mark -- he'll thrive playing off Stephen Curry (and LeBron James ?). The Warriors had a plus-3.9 net rating with Melton on the court last season, which ranked second on the team behind Jimmy Butler III . Still only 28 years old, he's squarely in his prime. Perhaps he'll turn in another solid season and do the "opt out and re-sign" dance with Golden State once again next summer. July 1: Lakers sign three players in half-hour span Quentin Grimes terms: Four years, $60 million Grade: B- Sandro Mamukelashvili terms: Four years, $52 million Grade: B Collin Sexton terms: Two years, $19 million (player option in second year) Grade: B- The Lakers piled all of their offseason activity into one hectic hour. After coming to an agreement on a blockbuster trade for center Walker Kessler , they signed these three role players in quick succession, dramatically reconfiguring their roster around Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves . LeBron James , Rui Hachimura , Marcus Smart and Luke Kennard were the top four Lakers in minutes played last postseason, but all four are now out, while Grimes, Mamukelashvili and Sexton are in.
